think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 43-year-old immunocompetent man presents precipitously with coma (Glasgow Coma Scale 8), fever, nuchal rigidity, markedly elevated CRP (242.5 mg/L), and neuroimaging showing layering suppurative intraventricular debris and ependymal enhancement. The clinical tension lies in differentiating acute pyogenic bacterial ventriculitis—the overwhelmingly common cause of purulent ventricular fluid—from an extraordinarily rare presentation of central nervous system tuberculosis presenting as primary pyogenic ventriculitis without basal arachnoiditis, hydrocephalus, or pulmonary involvement.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint is established immediately following emergent noncontrast CT and contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain demonstrating suppurative ventriculitis and fluid-fluid layering, prior to emergency external ventricular drainage (EVD), pus sampling, acid-fast bacillus staining, and GeneXpert PCR.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute pyogenic bacterial ventriculitis/meningitis was the primary initial diagnosis given the rapid onset, hyperpyrexia, high inflammatory markers, and intraventricular pus, prompting immediate third-generation cephalosporin administration, but was disproven when microbiological testing demonstrated acid-fast bacilli and positive GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Central nervous system neoplasm was excluded by the presence of acute purulent fluid rather than a solid neoplastic lesion on DWI/FLAIR and gross examination.
case_prompt:
A 43-year-old previously healthy man is brought to the emergency department after an acute onset of loss of consciousness. He has no known pre-existing medical conditions, and his past medical history is unremarkable. His family history is notable for the death of his father seven months earlier from a severe fatal pulmonary infection.

On arrival at the emergency department, his vital signs demonstrate a blood pressure of 118/85 mmHg, pulse rate of 78 beats per minute, and body temperature of 38.3 °C. Physical examination reveals a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 (E3V1M4) with prominent neck stiffness. He has no focal cranial nerve deficits or rash.

Initial triage laboratory investigations reveal a markedly elevated C-reactive protein of 242.5 mg/L. Retroviral serology is negative. A plain chest radiograph is normal.

Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the brain reveals enlargement of the left lateral ventricle containing an isodense lesion with minimal, fine, complete rim enhancement, suggestive of an intraventricular collection. Emergency magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain shows the left lateral ventricular lesion to have low signal intensity on T1-weighted imaging and high signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging, with thickened ependymal sheath enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced sequences. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences demonstrate layering of fluid and sediment within the ventricle, and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) reveals marked diffusion restriction in the posterior temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, consistent with suppurative fluid within the cerebral ventricles.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Strongly suspected given the acute obtundation, high fever, marked CRP elevation (242.5 mg/L), and suppurative intraventricular fluid on MRI prompting empiric third-generation cephalosporin therapy, but ruled out when pus bacteriological analysis revealed acid-fast bacilli and positive GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Empirical intravenous antibiotic treatment with third-generation cephalosporin (per-operative single dosage administration) was continued after surgery. The result of Ziehl-Neelsen staining to detect acid-fast bacteria in the pus sample was positive. GeneXpert was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to an intraventricular rim-enhancing mass causing unilateral ventricular enlargement, but refuted by marked fever, acute elevation of inflammatory markers, diffusion restriction with fluid-fluid layering indicating purulent debris rather than tumor, and aspiration of frank pus.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), the ventricle contains a layering of fluid and sediment. There was diffusion restriction in the posterior temporal horn of the lateral ventricle of the lesion, which was observed on diffusion-weighted imaging... These radiological findings suggested the presence of suppurative fluid in the cerebral ventricles.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Emergency placement of an external ventricular drain yielded thick cloudy pus; Ziehl-Neelsen staining was positive for acid-fast bacteria and GeneXpert PCR confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis, establishing primary tuberculous pyogenic ventriculitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A thick, cloudy, pus-like fluid emerged from the drain... The result of Ziehl-Neelsen staining to detect acid-fast bacteria in the pus sample was positive. GeneXpert was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Antibacillar treatment was started and then continued for a total of 12 months.

editor_comments: Strict admission breakpoint preserved at the emergency neuroimaging evaluation (CT and MRI), prior to surgical ventricular cannulation, external drainage, and microbiological/GeneXpert results. Zero pathogen names or spoilers in the presentation.
